old: First letter in the collection. Documents the 34th NY's journey from Albany to Washington in the opening weeks of the war, including passage through Baltimore — a city where a riot had killed soldiers just weeks earlier (April 19, 1861).

Already mindful of his widowed mother, he declines a costly furlough home, trusting she will need the eight dollars he sent more than he needs the visit.
final: Henry's first letter home: the 34th New York reaches Washington, cheered the whole way from Albany yet braced for trouble. FEEDBACK: This is a strong, well-grounded draft that earns its length and stays vivid. It nails the historical hook — a brand-new regiment's first passage through Baltimore, the very city where the 6th Massachusetts had been mobbed and bloodied that April, which is exactly why twenty men marched with loaded weapons and why the depot still bore bullet holes. The summary lets a knowing reader feel that tension without importing the outside event (per the no-outside-events rule), and the "rather cheered" detail is a lovely, precise period note that complicates the expected hostility. The human beat — declining the furlough so his mother keeps the eight dollars — lands naturally and is woven, not tacked on. Minor calibration: "an earlier row" slightly undersells; the letter's own language and the loaded-gun detail signal real, recent danger, so a word like "earlier trouble" or "earlier clash" carries the menace a hair better without spoiling or importing. The phrase "Already mindful of his widowed mother" is a touch editorial-explanatory; the act itself already shows the mindfulness. Both are polish, not problems.

old: Henry is writing from Washington while hearing the cannons of the First Battle of Bull Run (Manassas) — the first major battle of the Civil War, fought July 21, 1861, approximately 25-30 miles from Washington. This is a real-time eyewitness account of the battle's sound reaching the capital.
draft: Writing from Washington on July 21, 1861, Henry tells his mother that "while I am writing there is a battle going on," with cannons firing "not over twenty-eight miles from here" — a real-time eyewitness account of distant fighting. Every claim is anchored in the letter: the Washington, D.C. dateline; the 34th New York stationed "as guards to keep the rebels from crossing the river"; the relayed opinion the regiment "may never see a battle"; Henry's answer "I for one am willing to go. I don't care where"; the five-dollar gold piece sent home by the Capt. with the command to spend it; and the Co. The unit "34th New York" is supplied from collection metadata, not the letter text, but it is correct and the brief permits identifying the regiment, so this is acceptable framing rather than an invented fact.

FEEDBACK: The summary is accurate, period-correct, and well-chosen in its anchors. The 1861 Potomac picket-guard posting, the green-regiment anxiety about "never seeing a battle," and the camp-accident death are exactly the historically significant beats — they situate this firmly in the static, disease-and-drill first autumn of the war before the regiment ever faced combat, which a historian tracing the collection's arc needs. The three-quote density is the one real weakness: three direct quotations in 350-odd characters reads slightly as a quote-reel, and the gold-piece "command" line, while charming, is the least historically load-bearing. Two smaller notes: "rebel crossings" is period-apt phrasing and fine; and the letter's quiet undercurrent — Henry sick, unable to drill three days, in a camp that is "a great place for fever and ague" — is the human/historical beat actually most emblematic of 1861 camp life, and the draft omits it entirely in favor of the eager-for-battle line. That illness detail would deepen the period texture more than the gold-piece command. First, the draft slightly buries the human/moral beat that gives the letter its texture — Henry's anxiety that "it will go hard with" the rope-cutter, his sympathy even as he stays clear ("I am sorry for the man"), which is more revealing of the citizen-soldier's moral world than the bare phrase "keeps clear of trouble." Length and voice sit well within the rich target. Tighten "putting the whole company under arrest" to avoid the faint implication the comrade's act alone caused it; the arrest was the command's response to flush out the unknown cutter.

The "34th NY" is correct collection-level knowledge but is an imported fact. Per the brief (summary text must contain only facts found in THIS letter), naming "the 34th" is an out-of-letter insertion. Safer to write "his regiment" / "Henry's regiment."
- "lately dubbed 'the sharp shooters' in the papers" — supported ("I see in the papers we are called the sharp shooters").

The one real problem is the unit: the letter says only "our Regt.," so "the 34th" is an imported fact that violates the in-letter-only rule. Change it to "his regiment." Two small calibrations. First, "Capt. Second, the phrase "amid stove-buying, barracks-building" risks reading as a compressed topic-cluster; one of the three domestic items could be dropped to let the sentence breathe, but this is taste, not a defect. The voice is correct for an early-war (December 1861) camp letter, before the hard campaigning of 1862, when soldiers' chief concerns were comfort, pay, and news from home — the summary captures that register precisely.
